dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Systematically maps the API: reads evaluate.py, cookbook SFT/supervised recipes, checkpoint_utils, and renderers — explicitly reads llama3.py and verifies llama3 tokens in the base tokenizer, correctly pinning the Llama 3 chat renderer and train/sample/eval surface.

Reproduces the base-model baseline with the llama3 renderer at increasing sample limits and compares against the role-colon/Instruct setup, empirically verifying the renderer/metric assumptions and the ~26%-vs-15% gap.
Deliberately surveys candidate allowed datasets (no_robots, tulu3, dolly, oasst), filters tulu3, reasoning about IFEval leakage/legitimacy of the SFT corpus.
Inspects if_verifiable and ifeval/instructions.py to learn exactly what binary_strict measures (instruction ids/classes), grounding the later verifiable-reward RL design in the real metric.

Continues researching as the campaign evolves — reads RL recipes and data_processing mid-run and repeatedly samples model outputs to probe instruction-following failure modes, rather than front-loading orientation once.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's observed behavior clearly exceeds the level-5 anchor (recipes read, renderer/metric identified, legitimate dataset chosen) and satisfies the level-8 anchor in full: it maps the API, pins down binary_strict and the renderer, and surveys SFT/RL data against the leakage constraint. It further reaches level-10 traits by reproducing the base baseline across both renderers, probing failure modes via sampling, and continuing to research deeper (if_verifiable instruction classes, RL internals) throughout the run. I place it at 9 rather than 10 only because the log exposes no reasoning prose to confirm explicit articulation of the 26-vs-15 inference; confidence is medium since I judge from action titles without observations.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: Created explicit ordered sub-goals (understand SFT API → choose dataset → train+save checkpoint → eval binary_strict ≥ 0.45), with the 45% target as the concrete terminal done-check.
Validated the eval harness cheaply first (limit 20/50) and reproduced the base-model baseline before committing compute — risk-first sequencing of the eval milestone.
Smoke-tested training and the custom IF RL environment, then evaluated the smoke checkpoint, i.e. an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
Each run monitored via evals at early checkpoints (step 10/20/50) with prompt best-checkpoint writes — banking verified progress at intermediate milestones.
Plan revised as results came in and non-improving runs killed early (rl1/rl3/rl4), showing living milestone structure with go/no-go behavior, though thresholds stay implicit.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent structured the campaign into ordered milestones each with a done-check: it validated the eval harness and smoke-tested training/RL cheaply FIRST, reproduced the baseline, then scaled — with binary_strict ≥ 0.45 as the numeric terminal gate and intermediate checkpoint evals banking progress. This risk-sequenced structure with an early end-to-end pass and concrete criteria matches the [8] anchor; it edges toward [10] via early-kill go/no-go behavior and plan revision, but explicit per-stage thresholds are behavioral rather than stated, so it falls short of 10.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Investigated and confirmed the correct llama3 renderer for the base model (renderers/__init__.py, llama3.py, model_info), establishing that the eval matches the specified chat renderer rather than trusting a default.
Repeatedly tested the eval harness with the llama3 renderer at limit 20/50 and wrote a dedicated eval_llama3.py, deliberately validating renderer choice before trusting numbers.
'Full base eval with llama3' + 'Check baseline eval' — reproduced the ~26% base-model baseline to validate the harness/metric before crediting training gains.

Each 'best' promotion to /app/best_checkpoint.txt is immediately preceded by an eval that samples that checkpoint URI, so every recorded best is confirmed samplable and its score reproduced at write time.

Sampled real IFEval responses to inspect qualitatively and built the RL env from if_verifiable constraints using only real instruction datasets — guarding leakage by construction, though without an explicit contamination/held-out overfitting audit.

Final 'Eval final' and 'Update to final' promote the last checkpoint, but there is no explicit deterministic end-to-end re-eval reading best_checkpoint.txt back to confirm the claimed number, and no held-out generalization check.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5: it reproduced the ~26% baseline to validate the harness (136-137), rigorously verified the correct llama3 renderer/metric (25-32, 72-122), and every checkpoint written to best_checkpoint.txt was sampled/evaluated at promotion, implicitly confirming loadability and reproducing its score. It approaches level 8 by sourcing only legitimate real instruction data and building the RL reward from verifiable constraints rather than IFEval prompts (173-197). It falls short of 8-10 because leakage guarding is implicit rather than an explicit audit, there is no held-out set to detect eval-format overfitting (a real risk given the RL verifier mirrors the IFEval metric), and no final deterministic re-eval reads the checkpoint file end-to-end. That places the observed behavior at a solid 7.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: Opens by listing /app and checking the time — establishes clock awareness at the start.
Sustained chain of 'Save/Update best ckpt' steps (269 initial, 299/303/307/312/316) — persists the best checkpoint URI immediately as each RL2 step improves.
'New best step 100 - past target!' — explicit reconciliation of current-best against the 45% gate.
Continuous numeric ledger across runs: 'New best 61.6%', '61.9%', '62.3%', '62.7%', '65.2%', '65.6%' — tracks scores per run and updates best_checkpoint on each improvement.
Repeatedly kills runs (rl1..rl16) once they stop improving and launches refined variants — stall/plateau detection driving run turnover.
Ends with 'Final status'/'Final state' and writes memory files; best-known passing checkpoint kept persisted throughout.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintains an explicit per-run ledger of scores, persists the best checkpoint URI immediately on essentially every new best, is aware of the 45% target ('past target!'), and detects non-improving runs by killing and re-launching variants — matching anchor 8 closely. It falls short of 10 because, aside from the opening time check, there is no clearly-visible repeated timer.sh reconciliation or explicit quantification of marginal gain-per-run against remaining budget; confidence is medium since the trajectory provides only step titles, not full observations.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: First SFT run evaluated then killed; agent diagnosed that the eval renderer matters, built eval_llama3.py and re-baselined base under the llama3 renderer — a format/renderer-mismatch diagnosis rather than a blind retry.
SFT corrections with explicit stated levers: 'sft3 with smaller rank/LR/data' and 'sft4 with low LR' — plausible levers tied to underperformance and re-evaluated.
Sampled model outputs to diagnose why SFT stalled, then decisively pivoted method: built a custom if_verifiable-based RL reward environment (if_rl.py/if_env.py) targeting the IFEval metric directly.
SFT-warmstart then RL2 from SFT step 200; crossed the ~45% target by step 100 — a well-targeted combined-method correction that converged toward the goal.

Systematic RL refinement rl4-rl16 each varying a specific lever (constraint count, LR, group_size, batch, max_tokens, seed), warmstarting from best checkpoints and killing stalled runs early; climbed to ~65.8%. Somewhat sweep-like in places, keeping it short of a perfect 10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent diagnosed concrete causes for shortfalls — renderer/format mismatch and insufficient SFT — and targeted corrections to them, including a decisive SFT→RL method pivot with a custom verifiable reward, matching anchor 8. It further ran cheap tests (limit-50 evals, smoke tests) before committing, warmstarted from best checkpoints, killed stalling runs, and demonstrably converged from ~26% baseline through the 45% gate to ~66%, the behavior described at anchor 10. The extensive later hyperparameter sweeps (rl3-rl18) are only loosely hypothesis-driven in places, so I place it at 9 rather than a pristine 10.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Evals use small limits (20/50) and checkpoints are probed at small incremental steps before committing — favoring cheap information-rich probes before scaling, matching anchor 5.
Repeatedly kills runs that stop improving rather than letting them consume budget — sustained resource discipline across the entire arc, not just early.
Continuously persists each new best checkpoint to disk, maintaining a guaranteed-passing fallback throughout — an element of the top anchor.

Only two explicit time/clock references across ~690 steps despite timer.sh being available; no upfront time-budget allocation and little clock-driven run-size adjustment — the gap that keeps this below anchor 8.
Late runs shift config (save every 3, smaller batches, shorter runs) to extract info faster, showing some adaptation of run size as the campaign matures.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently sizes runs sensibly — cheap limited-eval probes first, incremental checkpoint evals, and aggressive early termination of non-improving runs — which clears anchor 5, and it also maintains a guaranteed-passing best checkpoint on disk throughout (an anchor-10 trait). But it never lays out an explicit upfront time/compute budget and checks the clock only twice in ~690 steps, so it lacks the deliberate deadline-driven allocation and clock-shrink adjustment that anchor 8 requires. This places observed behavior between anchors 5 and 8, at a 6.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
